facts.statement: Dilophosaurus lived during the Early Jurassic period, specifically from the Sinemurian to Toarcian stages.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Early Jurassic (Sinemurian–Toarcian),

facts.statement: Three Dilophosaurus skeletons were discovered in northern Arizona in 1940, with the two best-preserved ones collected in 1942.
facts.quote: Three skeletons were discovered in northern Arizona in 1940, and the two best preserved were collected in 1942.

facts.statement: Samuel P. Welles named the most complete specimen *Megalosaurus wetherilli* in 1954.
facts.quote: The most complete specimen became the holotype of a new species in the genus Megalosaurus, named M. wetherilli by Samuel P. Welles in 1954.

facts.statement: Welles discovered a larger skeleton of the same species in 1964 in the same region.
facts.quote: Welles found a larger skeleton in the same region belonging to the same species in 1964.

facts.statement: Welles reclassified the species into the new genus *Dilophosaurus* in 1970 after realizing it had skull crests.
facts.quote: Realizing it bore crests on its skull, he assigned the species to the new genus Dilophosaurus in 1970, as Dilophosaurus wetherilli.

facts.statement: Dilophosaurus had long, curved, thin, and sideways-compressed teeth, with lower jaw teeth being much smaller than upper jaw teeth.
facts.quote: The teeth were long, curved, thin, and compressed sideways. Those in the lower jaw were much smaller than those of the upper jaw.

facts.statement: Dilophosaurus hands had four fingers: a short, strong first finger with a large claw, two longer slender fingers with smaller claws, and a vestigial fourth finger.
facts.quote: The hands had four fingers; the first was short but strong and bore a large claw, the two following fingers were longer and slenderer with smaller claws; the fourth was vestigial.

facts.statement: Dilophosaurus was likely an active, bipedal predator that may have hunted large animals but also fed on smaller animals and fish.
facts.quote: Dilophosaurus would have been active and bipedal, and may have hunted large animals; it could also have fed on smaller animals and fish.

facts.statement: Dilophosaurus may have grown rapidly, reaching a growth rate of 30 to 35 kilograms per year early in life.
facts.quote: It may have grown rapidly, attaining a growth rate of 30 to 35 kg per year early in life.

facts.statement: Dilophosaurus is known from the Kayenta Formation and lived alongside dinosaurs like *Scutellosaurus* and *Sarahsaurus*.
facts.quote: Dilophosaurus is known from the Kayenta Formation, and lived alongside dinosaurs such as Scutellosaurus and Sarahsaurus.

facts.statement: In the summer of 1942, paleontologist Charles L. Camp led a UCMP field party to search for fossils in Navajo County, northern Arizona.
facts.quote: In the summer of 1942, the paleontologist Charles L. Camp led a field party from the University of California Museum of Paleontology (UCMP) in search of fossil vertebrates in Navajo County in northern Arizona.

facts.statement: Three Dilophosaurus skeletons were found arranged in a triangle about 30 feet long in purplish shale.
facts.quote: Three dinosaur skeletons were found in purplish shale, arranged in a triangle, about 30 ft long at one side.

facts.statement: Cleaning and mounting the first nearly complete specimen at UCMP under Wann Langston took three men two years.
facts.quote: The nearly complete first specimen was cleaned and mounted at the UCMP under supervision of the paleontologist Wann Langston, a process that took three men two years.

facts.statement: Specimen UCMP 37302 was designated the holotype and UCMP 37303 the paratype for the species.
facts.quote: The nearly complete specimen (catalogued as UCMP 37302) was made the holotype of the species, and the second specimen (UCMP 37303) was made the paratype.

facts.statement: Welles initially placed the species in *Megalosaurus* due to similar limb proportions with *M. bucklandii* and a lack of perceived differences.
facts.quote: Welles placed the new species in Megalosaurus due to the similar limb proportions of it and M. bucklandii, and because he did not find great differences between them.

facts.statement: In 1964, Welles returned to Tuba City to date the Kayenta Formation and discovered another skeleton about 1/4 mile south of the 1942 finds.
facts.quote: Welles returned to Tuba City in 1964 to determine the age of the Kayenta Formation (it had been suggested to be Late Triassic in age, whereas Welles thought it was Early to Middle Jurassic), and discovered another skeleton about 1/4 mi south of where the 1942 specimens had been found.

facts.statement: Specimen UCMP 77270 was collected with the help of William J. Breed from the Museum of Northern Arizona.
facts.quote: The nearly complete specimen (catalogued as UCMP 77270) was collected with the help of William J. Breed of the Museum of Northern Arizona and others.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Dilophosaurus belongs to the family Dilophosauridae with *Dracovenator*, as some researchers do not support this grouping.
facts.quote: Dilophosaurus has been considered a member of the family Dilophosauridae along with Dracovenator, a group placed between the Coelophysidae and later theropods, but some researchers have not found support for this grouping.

facts.statement: The genus name Dilophosaurus means "two-crested lizard" and was coined by Welles in 1970.
facts.quote: In 1970, Welles coined the new genus name Dilophosaurus, from the Greek words di (δι) meaning "two", lophos (λόφος) meaning "crest", and sauros (σαυρος) meaning "lizard": "two-crested lizard".

facts.statement: In 2020, Marsh and Rowe comprehensively redescribed Dilophosaurus, including the previously undescribed specimen UCMP 77270.
facts.quote: In 2020, the paleontologists Adam D. Marsh and Timothy B. Rowe comprehensively redescribed Dilophosaurus based on the by then known specimens, including specimen UCMP 77270 which had remained undescribed since 1964.

facts.statement: Adam Marsh described Dilophosaurus as the "best worst-known dinosaur" because it remained poorly understood despite being discovered 80 years prior to his study.
facts.quote: In an interview, Marsh called Dilophosaurus the "best worst-known dinosaur", since the animal was poorly understood despite having been discovered 80 years earlier.

facts.statement: Marsh and Rowe concluded in 2020 that all known Dilophosaurus specimens belong to a single taxon, with differences explained by maturity and preservation.
facts.quote: Marsh and Rowe concluded in 2020 that there was only one taxon among known Dilophosaurus specimens, and that differences between them were due to their different degree of maturity and preservation.

facts.statement: A skeleton discovered in China in 1987 was initially named Dilophosaurus sinensis but was later found to be identical to Sinosaurus triassicus.
facts.quote: A nearly complete theropod skeleton (KMV 8701) was discovered in the Lufeng Formation, in Yunnan Province, China, in 1987. It is similar to Dilophosaurus, with a pair of crests and a gap separating the premaxilla from the maxilla, but differs in some details.

facts.statement: Dilophosaurus was the largest-known land animal in North America during the Early Jurassic.
facts.quote: It was also the largest-known land animal of North America during the Early Jurassic.

facts.statement: Dilophosaurus was slender and lightly built, with a size comparable to a brown bear.
facts.quote: Slender and lightly built, its size was comparable to that of a brown bear.

facts.statement: The largest-known Dilophosaurus specimen weighed approximately 400 kg, measured about 7 meters in length, and had a skull 590 mm long.
facts.quote: The largest-known specimen weighed about 400 kg, measured about 7 m in length, and its skull was 590 mm long.

facts.statement: Some researchers interpret a resting trace of a Dilophosaurus-like theropod as showing impressions of down-like feathers around the belly and feet.
facts.quote: A resting trace of a theropod similar to Dilophosaurus and Liliensternus has been interpreted by some researchers as showing impressions of feathers around the belly and feet, similar to down.

facts.statement: Other researchers interpret the same trackway impressions as sedimentological artifacts, though this does not definitively rule out the presence of feathers.
facts.quote: Other researchers instead interpret these impressions as sedimentological artifacts created as the dinosaur moved, though this interpretation does not rule out that the track-maker could have borne feathers.

facts.statement: Dilophosaurus possessed a pair of high, thin, arched crests running along the top of its skull.
facts.quote: Dilophosaurus bore a pair of high, thin, and arched (or plate-shaped) crests longitudinally on the skull roof.

facts.statement: The crests were formed primarily by the expanded nasal and lacrimal bones starting as low ridges on the premaxillae.
facts.quote: The crests (termed the nasolacrimal crests) began as low ridges on the premaxillae and were mainly formed by the upwards expanded nasal and lacrimal bones.

facts.statement: Researchers estimate the crests may have extended up to 12 mm above the skull based on preserved bone fragments.
facts.quote: Since only a short part of the upper surface of this process is unbroken, the rest of the crest may have risen above the skull over a distance of ~12 mm.

facts.statement: Scientists have debated whether the crests were covered in keratin or keratinized skin, comparing them to the double-crested cassowary.
facts.quote: Welles found the crests reminiscent of a double-crested cassowary, while Marsh and Rowe stated they were probably covered in keratin or keratinized skin.

facts.statement: CT scans reveal that air sacs were present in the skull bones surrounding the brain and connected to frontal sinus cavities.
facts.quote: CT scans show that air sacs (pockets of air that provide strength for and lighten bones) were present in the bones that surrounded the brain, and were continuous with the sinus cavities in the front of the skull.

facts.statement: Dilophosaurus nostrils were positioned further back on the skull than in most other theropod dinosaurs.
facts.quote: The nostrils were placed further back than in most other theropods.

facts.statement: A gap in the upper jaw known as the subnarial gap created a diastema, or notch, in the tooth row.
facts.quote: The subnarial gap resulted in a diastema, a gap in the tooth row (which has also been called a "notch").

facts.statement: The lower jaw was slender at the front but became massive at the connection to the skull and deep around the side opening.
facts.quote: The mandible was slender at the front, but the articular region (where it connected with the skull) was massive, and the mandible was deep around the mandibular fenestra (an opening on its side).

facts.statement: The front part of the lower jaw featured an up-curved chin rather than a pointed one.
facts.quote: The dentary bone (the front part of the mandible where most of the teeth there were attached) had an up-curved rather than pointed chin.

facts.statement: A unique pyramidal process on the surangular bone formed a horizontal shelf near the jaw joint.
facts.quote: The side surface of the surangular bone had a unique pyramidal process in front of the articulation with the quadrate, and this horizontal ridge formed a shelf.

facts.statement: Dilophosaurus had a long backward projection at the rear of the lower jaw.
facts.quote: The retroarticular process of the mandible (a backwards projection) was long.

facts.statement: Dilophosaurus possessed 10 neck vertebrae, 14 back vertebrae, and 45 tail vertebrae containing air sacs.
facts.quote: Dilophosaurus had 10 cervical (neck), 14 dorsal (back), and 45 caudal (tail) vertebrae, and air sacs grew into the vertebrae.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Dilophosaurus could flex its long neck nearly 90 degrees to hold its skull in a horizontal position.
facts.quote: It had a long neck, which was probably flexed nearly 90° by the skull and by the shoulder, holding the skull in a horizontal posture.

facts.statement: The tail vertebrae of Dilophosaurus had consistent lengths but narrowed in diameter from elliptical to circular cross-sections towards the rear.
facts.quote: The centra of the caudal vertebrae were very consistent in length, but their diameter became smaller towards the back, and they went from elliptical to circular in cross-section.

facts.statement: Dilophosaurus had uniquely wide shoulder blades with a rectangular or squared-off upper section.
facts.quote: The scapulae were wide, particularly the upper part, which was rectangular (or squared off), a unique feature.

facts.statement: A unique horizontal buttress next to the biceps tuber is found on the lower hind portions of Dilophosaurus coracoids.
facts.quote: The lower hind portions of the coracoids had a "horizontal buttress" next to the biceps tuber, unique for this genus.

facts.statement: Dilophosaurus hands had four fingers, with the first being shorter but stronger with a large claw, while the other two were longer and slenderer with smaller claws.
facts.quote: The hands had four fingers: the first was shorter but stronger than the following two fingers, with a large claw, and the two following fingers were longer and slenderer, with smaller claws.

facts.statement: The fourth finger of Dilophosaurus was vestigial, retained but without function, while the third finger was reduced.
facts.quote: The third finger was reduced, and the fourth was vestigial (retained, but without function).

facts.statement: Dilophosaurus had large hind legs where the thigh bone was slightly longer than the lower leg bone, unlike Coelophysis.
facts.quote: The hind legs were large, with a slighter longer femur (thigh bone) than tibia (lower leg bone), the opposite of, for example, Coelophysis.

facts.statement: The massive femur of Dilophosaurus had an S-shaped shaft with a greater trochanter centered on it.
facts.quote: The femur was massive; its shaft was sigmoid-shaped (curved like an 'S'), and its greater trochanter was centered on the shaft.

facts.statement: Dilophosaurus feet were long and stout with three well-developed toes bearing large claws that were much less curved than the hand claws.
facts.quote: It had long, stout feet with three well-developed toes that bore large claws, which were much less curved than those of the hand.

facts.statement: The third toe was the stoutest on Dilophosaurus, while the smaller first toe (hallux) was kept off the ground.
facts.quote: The third toe was the stoutest, and the smaller first toe (the hallux) was kept off the ground.

facts.statement: In 1970, paleontologist Welles revised his earlier 1954 classification of Dilophosaurus as a megalosaur after discovering it possessed crests.
facts.quote: Welles thought Dilophosaurus a megalosaur in 1954, but revised his opinion in 1970 after discovering that it had crests.

facts.statement: By 1974, Welles and Robert A. Long classified Dilophosaurus as a ceratosauroid.
facts.quote: By 1974, Welles and the paleontologist Robert A. Long found Dilophosaurus to be a ceratosauroid.

facts.statement: In 1984, Welles suggested that the division of theropods into Coelurosauria and Carnosauria based on body size was inaccurate because Dilophosaurus showed features of both groups.
facts.quote: In 1984 Welles found that Dilophosaurus exhibited features of both Coelurosauria and Carnosauria, the two main groups into which theropods had hitherto been divided, based on body size, and he suggested this division was inaccurate.

facts.statement: In 1988, Gregory S. Paul suggested that Dilophosaurus might be a direct descendant of Coelophysis.
facts.quote: In 1988, paleontologist Gregory S. Paul classified the halticosaurs as a subfamily of the family Coelophysidae, and suggested that Dilophosaurus could have been a direct descendant of Coelophysis.

facts.statement: In 1994, Thomas R. Holtz placed Dilophosaurus in the group Coelophysoidea within Ceratosauria, separate from the family Coelophysidae.
facts.quote: In 1994, paleontologist Thomas R. Holtz placed Dilophosaurus in the group Coelophysoidea, along with but separate from the Coelophysidae. He placed the Coelophysoidea in the group Ceratosauria.

facts.statement: In 2000, James H. Madsen and Welles established the family Dilophosauridae containing only Dilophosaurus.
facts.quote: In 2000, paleontologist James H. Madsen and Welles divided Ceratosauria into the families Ceratosauridae and Dilophosauridae, with Dilophosaurus as the sole member of the latter family.

facts.statement: In 1998, Lamanna and colleagues noted that cranial crests are not unique to Dilophosaurus and have limited use for determining relationships among theropods.
facts.quote: Lamanna and colleagues pointed out in 1998 that since Dilophosaurus was discovered to have had crests on its skull, other similarly crested theropods have been discovered (including Sinosaurus), and that this feature is, therefore, not unique to the genus, and of limited use for determining interrelationships within their group.

facts.statement: In 2005, Adam M. Yates found the South African genus Dracovenator to be closely related to Dilophosaurus and Zupaysaurus.
facts.quote: Paleontologist Adam M. Yates described the genus Dracovenator from South Africa in 2005, and found it closely related to Dilophosaurus and Zupaysaurus.

facts.statement: In 2007, Nathan D. Smith and colleagues identified Cryolophosaurus as the sister species of Dilophosaurus.
facts.quote: In 2007, paleontologist Nathan D. Smith and colleagues found the crested theropod Cryolophosaurus to be the sister species of Dilophosaurus, and grouped them with Dracovenator and Sinosaurus.

facts.statement: In 2012, Carrano and colleagues concluded that Dilophosaurus was a coelophysoid, while Cryolophosaurus and Sinosaurus were more derived basal members of Tetanurae.
facts.quote: In 2012, Carrano and colleagues found that the group of crested theropods proposed by Smith and colleagues was based on features that relate to the presence of such crests, but that the features of the rest of the skeleton were less consistent. They instead found that Dilophosaurus was a coelophysoid, with Cryolophosaurus and Sinosaurus being more derived, as basal members of the group Tetanurae.

facts.statement: In 2015, Christophe Hendrickx and colleagues defined Dilophosauridae to include Dilophosaurus and Dracovenator as the sister group to Averostra.
facts.quote: Paleontologist Christophe Hendrickx and colleagues defined the Dilophosauridae to include Dilophosaurus and Dracovenator in 2015, and noted that while general uncertainty exists about the placement of this group, it appears to be slightly more derived than the Coelophysoidea, and the sister group to the Averostra.

facts.statement: In 2019, Zahner and Brinkmann found that Dilophosauridae members were successive basal sister taxa of Averostra rather than a single monophyletic clade.
facts.quote: In 2019, paleontologists Marion Zahner and Winand Brinkmann found the members of the Dilophosauridae to be successive basal sister taxa of the Averostra rather than a monophyletic clade (a natural group), but noted that some of their analyses did find the group valid, containing Dilophosaurus, Dracovenator, Cryolophosaurus, and possibly Notatesseraeraptor as the basal-most member.

facts.statement: In 2020, Marsh and Rowe found no support for Dilophosauridae and suggested cranial crests were an ancestral trait of Ceratosauria and Tetanurae.
facts.quote: In the phylogenetic analysis accompanying their 2020 redescription, Marsh and Rowe found all specimens of Dilophosaurus to form a monophyletic group, sister to Averostra, and more derived than Cryolophosaurus. Their analysis did not find support for Dilophosauridae, and they suggested cranial crests were a plesiomorphic (ancestral) trait of Ceratosauria and Tetanurae.

facts.statement: In 1971, paleontologist Welles reported dinosaur footprints from the Kayenta Formation in northern Arizona located 45 ft and 367 ft below the original Dilophosaurus specimens.
facts.quote: In 1971, Welles reported dinosaur footprints from the Kayenta Formation of northern Arizona, on two levels 45 ft and 367 ft below where the original Dilophosaurus specimens were found.

facts.statement: Welles named the ichnospecies Dilophosauripus williamsi based on tridactyl footprints that could have been made by Dilophosaurus.
facts.quote: The lower footprints were tridactyl (three-toed), and could have been made by Dilophosaurus; Welles created the new ichnogenus and species Dilophosauripus williamsi based on them, in honor of Williams, the discoverer of the first Dilophosaurus skeletons.

facts.statement: In 1996, Morales and Bulkey estimated that a trackmaker of the ichnogenus Eubrontes would have been 2.83 to 2.99 m tall at the hips, making it unlikely to be Dilophosaurus, which stands 1.50 to 1.75 m tall.
facts.quote: In 1996, the paleontologists Michael Morales and Scott Bulkey reported a trackway of the ichnogenus Eubrontes from the Kayenta Formation made by a very large theropod. They noted it could have been made by a very large Dilophosaurus individual, but found that unlikely, as they estimated the trackmaker would have been 2.83 - 2.99 m tall at the hips, compared to the 1.50 - 1.75 m of Dilophosaurus.

facts.statement: In 1991, paleontologist Gerard Gierliński concluded that tridactyl footprints from the Holy Cross Mountains in Poland belonged to a theropod similar to Dilophosaurus.
facts.quote: The paleontologist Gerard Gierliński examined tridactyl footprints from the Holy Cross Mountains in Poland and concluded in 1991 that they belonged to a theropod like Dilophosaurus.

facts.statement: Gierliński and Sabath argued in 2005 that traces resembling modern bird semiplumes found on a track were real feather impressions, not sedimentological artifacts, based on experiments showing algae mats leave similar marks.
facts.quote: Martin and colleagues also reassigned the track to the ichnotaxon Fulicopus lyellii. Gierliński and Karol Sabath responded at a conference talk in 2005, pointing out that the algae mat imprint would not only have been present on the stomach, but also the footprints. Based on detailed photos and experiments, they found the traces similar to those left by the fibrous feathers (semiplumes) of modern birds, and different from those left by a scaly body.

facts.statement: In 2003, Robert E. Weems proposed that Eubrontes tracks were made by a sauropodomorph similar to Plateosaurus rather than a theropod like Dilophosaurus.
facts.quote: The paleontologist Robert E. Weems proposed in 2003 that Eubrontes tracks were not produced by a theropod, but by a sauropodomorph similar to Plateosaurus, excluding Dilophosaurus as a possible trackmaker.

facts.statement: Weems suggested that rounded impressions in some trackways represented hand impressions indicating quadrupedal movement.
facts.quote: Weems suggested rounded impressions associated with some of these trackways to represent hand impressions lacking digit traces, which he interpreted as a trace of quadrupedal movement.

facts.statement: In 2019, Weems argued that Eubrontes tracks were made by the bipedal sauropodomorph Anchisaurus rather than reflecting the gracile feet of Dilophosaurus.
facts.quote: Weems stated in 2019 that Eubrontes tracks do not reflect the gracile feet of Dilophosaurus, and argued they were instead made by the bipedal sauropodomorph Anchisaurus.

facts.statement: In a 2024 review, John R. Foster and colleagues noted that few ichnologists accepted Weems' sauropodomorph interpretation of Eubrontes because the tracks are found where no sauropodomorph fossils exist.
facts.quote: In a 2024 review of Jurassic tracks, the paleontologist John R. Foster and colleagues stated that few other ichnologists had accepted Weems' sauropodomorph interpretation of Eubrontes, partially because such tracks are abundant in places where no sauropodomorph fossils have been found.

facts.statement: Early researcher Welles concluded that Dilophosaurus lacked a powerful bite because of a weak area in the snout called the subnarial gap.
facts.quote: Welles found that Dilophosaurus did not have a powerful bite, due to weakness caused by the subnarial gap.

facts.statement: Welles hypothesized that Dilophosaurus used front teeth for plucking and tearing while using rear teeth for piercing and slicing.
facts.quote: He thought that it used its front premaxillary teeth for plucking and tearing rather than biting, and the maxillary teeth further back for piercing and slicing.

facts.statement: Welles suggested that Dilophosaurus was likely a scavenger that killed large animals using its hands and feet instead of its jaws.
facts.quote: He thought that it was probably a scavenger rather than a predator, and that if it did kill large animals, it would have done so with its hands and feet rather than its jaws.

facts.statement: In 1986, Robert T. Bakker argued that Dilophosaurus was adapted to kill large prey and could attack Early Jurassic herbivores.
facts.quote: In 1986, the paleontologist Robert T. Bakker instead found Dilophosaurus, with its massive neck and skull and large upper teeth, to have been adapted for killing large prey, and strong enough to attack any Early Jurassic herbivores.

facts.statement: Therrien and colleagues suggested that if Dilophosaurus fed on small prey, any hunting packs would have been limited in size.
facts.quote: The authors suggested that if Dilophosaurus indeed fed on small prey, possible hunting packs would have been of limited size.

facts.statement: In 2007, Milner and James I. Kirkland suggested that features of Dilophosaurus indicate it may have eaten fish.
facts.quote: Milner and paleontologist James I. Kirkland suggested in 2007 that Dilophosaurus had features that indicate it may have eaten fish.

facts.statement: Milner and Kirkland noted that Dilophosaurus had jaw ends expanded into a 'rosette' of teeth similar to fish-eating spinosaurids and gharials.
facts.quote: They pointed out that the ends of the jaws were expanded to the sides, forming a "rosette" of interlocking teeth, similar to those of spinosaurids, known to have eaten fish, and gharials, which is the modern crocodile that eats the most fish.

facts.statement: In 2020, Marsh and Rowe suggested that features distinguishing Dilophosaurus from earlier theropods were linked to increased body size and preying on large animals.
facts.quote: Marsh and Rowe suggested in 2020 that many of the features that distinguished Dilophosaurus from earlier theropods were associated with increased body size and macropredation (preying on large animals).

facts.statement: Fleshy air sacs in Dilophosaurus's vertebrae strengthened and lightened its skeleton while allowing unidirectional airflow for more oxygen than mammals.
facts.quote: The fleshy air sacs from its respiratory system that grew into the vertebrae both strengthened and lightened the skeleton, and allowed unidirectional airflow through its lungs, similar to birds and crocodiles, and thereby more oxygen than a bidirectional respiratory system of mammals (wherein the air flows in and out of the lungs).

facts.statement: Unidirectional breathing suggests Dilophosaurus had high metabolic rates and was likely a fast, agile hunter.
facts.quote: Unidirectional breathing indicates relatively high metabolic rates and therefore high levels of activity, indicating that Dilophosaurus was likely a fast, agile hunter.

facts.statement: Brown and Rowe considered Dilophosaurus to be an apex predator in its ecosystem rather than a scavenger.
facts.quote: Brown and Rowe considered Dilophosaurus to have been an apex predator in its ecosystem, and not a scavenger.

facts.statement: Dilophosaurus had powerful, flexible forelimbs that were not used for walking.
facts.quote: He found the forelimbs to have been powerful weapons, strong and flexible, and not used for locomotion.

facts.statement: The hands of Dilophosaurus could grasp, slash, meet each other, and reach two-thirds of the way up the neck.
facts.quote: He noted that the hands were capable of grasping and slashing, of meeting each other, and reaching two-thirds up the neck.

facts.statement: In 1990, Stephen and Sylvia Czerkas hypothesized that the weak pelvis of Dilophosaurus might indicate an aquatic lifestyle and efficient swimming ability.
facts.quote: In 1990, paleontologists Stephen and Sylvia Czerkas suggested that the weak pelvis of Dilophosaurus could have been an adaptation for an aquatic lifestyle, where the water would help support its weight, and that it could have been an efficient swimmer.

facts.statement: In 1998, Per Christiansen estimated the top speed of Dilophosaurus to be between 43 and 69 km per hour.
facts.quote: In 1998, paleontologist Per Christiansen estimated the top speed of Dilophosaurus to have been 43 - 69 km per hour.

facts.statement: Research by Phil Senter and James H. Robins found that Dilophosaurus could retract its humerus almost parallel to the scapula but could not move it forward beyond a vertical orientation.
facts.quote: They found that Dilophosaurus would have been able to draw its humerus backward until it was almost parallel with the scapula, but could not move it forwards to a more than vertical orientation.

facts.statement: The fingers of Dilophosaurus were likely not voluntarily hyperextensible but may have been passively hyperextensible to prevent dislocation during prey struggles.
facts.quote: The fingers do not appear to have been voluntarily hyperextensible (able to extend backwards, beyond their normal range), but they may have been passively hyperextensible, to resist dislocation during violent movements by captured prey.

facts.statement: Experiments by Senter and Sullivan showed the humerus of Dilophosaurus could be elevated 65 degrees and protracted to an almost vertical level.
facts.quote: They found that the humerus of Dilophosaurus could be retracted into a position that was almost parallel with the scapula, protracted to an almost vertical level, and elevated 65°.

facts.statement: The wrist structure of Dilophosaurus prevented pronation and supination, causing the palms to face medially toward each other.
facts.quote: Pronation and supination of the wrists (crossing the radius and ulna bones of the lower arm to turn the hand) was prevented by the radius and ulna joints not being able to roll, and the palms, therefore, faced medially, towards each other.

facts.statement: Senter and Sullivan concluded Dilophosaurus could grip objects with two hands, hold small items in one hand, seize prey beneath the chest, and perform displays by swinging its arms.
facts.quote: Senter and Sullivan concluded that Dilophosaurus was able to grip and hold objects between two hands, to grip and hold small objects in one hand, to seize objects close beneath the chest, to bring an object to the mouth, to perform a display by swinging the arms in an arc along the sides of the ribcage, to scratch the chest, belly, or the half of the other forelimb farthest from the body, to seize prey beneath the chest or the base of the neck, and to clutch objects to the chest.

facts.statement: The hyperextensibility of Dilophosaurus fingers may have protected them from dislocation during prey struggles without aiding locomotion.
facts.quote: The hyperextensibility of the fingers may have prevented the prey's violent struggle from dislocating them, since it would have allowed greater motion of the fingers (with no importance to locomotion).

facts.statement: The short forelimbs and limited shoulder mobility suggest Dilophosaurus used its mouth to make first contact with prey rather than its hands.
facts.quote: The limited mobility of the shoulder and shortness of the forelimbs indicates that the mouth made first contact with the prey rather than the hands.

facts.statement: John Welles suggested that the crests of Dilophosaurus might have been used for thermoregulation despite lacking vascular grooves, though he admitted this was conjectural.
facts.quote: Welles conceded that suggestions as to the function of the crests of Dilophosaurus were conjectural, but thought that, though the crests had no grooves to indicate vascularization, they could have been used for thermoregulation.

facts.statement: In 1986, Bakker proposed that the thin crests of Dilophosaurus were sexual adornments for visual effect, unlike the thicker crests of allosaurs used for head-butting.
facts.quote: Bakker considered the crests sexual adornments in 1986, noting they were so thin that they could only have been for visual effect, unlike the heavier crests of allosaurs, which could have been used for head-butting.

facts.statement: In 1990, Stephen and Sylvia Czerkas argued that the delicate structure of Dilophosaurus crests made them unsuitable for battle.
facts.quote: The Czerkas pointed out in 1990 that the crests could not have been used during battle, as their delicate structure would have been easily damaged.

facts.statement: In 2011, Kevin Padian and John R. Horner proposed that bizarre cranial structures in dinosaurs like Dilophosaurus were primarily for species recognition, dismissing other functions.
facts.quote: In 2011 the paleontologists Kevin Padian and John R. Horner proposed that "bizarre structures" in dinosaurs in general (including crests, frills, horns, and domes) were primarily used for species recognition, and dismissed other explanations as unsupported by evidence.

facts.statement: In 2020, Marsh and Rowe agreed that Dilophosaurus crests likely played a role in species identification or sexual selection, similar to modern birds.
facts.quote: Marsh and Rowe agreed in 2020 that the crests of Dilophosaurus likely had a role in species identification or intersexual/intrasexual selection, as in some modern birds.

facts.statement: The original describer, Welles, initially thought the smaller fossils were juveniles and the larger one an adult, but later considered them different species.
facts.quote: Welles originally interpreted the smaller Dilophosaurus specimens as juveniles, and the larger specimen as an adult, later interpreting them as different species.

facts.statement: Paul proposed that size differences between Dilophosaurus specimens might represent sexual dimorphism, similar to what is seen in Coelophysis.
facts.quote: Paul suggested that the differences between the specimens was perhaps due to sexual dimorphism, as was seemingly also apparent in Coelophysis

facts.statement: In 2005, Gay found no evidence for sexual dimorphism in Dilophosaurus and instead attributed specimen differences to individual variation and growth changes.
facts.quote: In 2005 Gay found no evidence of the sexual dimorphism suggested by Paul (but supposedly present in Coelophysis), and attributed the variation seen between Dilophosaurus specimens to individual variation and ontogeny

facts.statement: Yates tentatively linked tiny nasal crests on a juvenile to the genus Dracovenator and suggested these crests would grow larger in adults.
facts.quote: Based on the tiny nasal crests on a juvenile specimen, Yates had tentatively assigned to the related genus Dracovenator, he suggested that these would have grown larger as the animal became adult.

facts.statement: Bone structure analysis suggests Dilophosaurus grew rapidly, potentially gaining 30 to 35 kg per year during early life.
facts.quote: The plexiform (woven) structure of the bones suggested rapid growth, and Dilophosaurus may have attained a growth rate of 30 to 35 kg per year early in life.

facts.statement: Welles observed that replacement teeth in Dilophosaurus originated deep within the bone and decreased in size with distance from the gum line.
facts.quote: Welles found that the replacement teeth of Dilophosaurus and other theropods originated deep inside the bone, decreasing in size the farther they were from the alveolar border.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen showed a groove on a neck vertebra possibly caused by injury and pits on the right arm bone that could be abscesses or artifacts.
facts.quote: The holotype had a sulcus (groove or furrow) on the neural arch of a cervical vertebra that may have been due to an injury or crushing, and two pits on the right humerus that may have been abscesses (collections of pus) or artifacts.

facts.statement: In 2001, Molnar suggested that asymmetry in the holotype's limbs was caused by a developmental anomaly known as fluctuating asymmetry.
facts.quote: In 2001, paleontologist Ralph Molnar suggested that this was caused by a developmental anomaly called fluctuating asymmetry.

facts.statement: A 2016 study found the Dilophosaurus holotype had the most varied and numerous diseases on its shoulder and forelimbs of any known theropod dinosaur.
facts.quote: In 2016 Senter and Sara L. Juengst examined the paleopathologies of the holotype specimen and found that it bore the greatest and most varied number of such maladies on the pectoral girdle and forelimb of any theropod dinosaur so far described

facts.statement: The Dilophosaurus holotype had eight diseased bones, a count higher than the maximum of four found in any other theropod specimen.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen had eight afflicted bones, whereas no other theropod specimen is known with more than four.

facts.statement: The holotype suffered a fractured shoulder blade and forearm bone on the left side, along with abscess-like infections in the ulna and thumb bone.
facts.quote: On its left side, it had a fractured scapula and radius, and fibriscesses (like abscesses) in the ulna and the outer phalanx bone of the thumb.

facts.statement: On the right side, the holotype had a twisted arm bone, three tumors on the forearm bone, a shortened joint surface on a hand bone, and deformities on a finger bone.
facts.quote: On the right side it had torsion of its humeral shaft, three bony tumors on its radius, a truncated articular surface of its third metacarpal bone, and deformities on the first phalanx bone of the third finger.

facts.statement: Deformities in the arm and finger bones may have been caused by osteodysplasia, a disease previously unknown in non-bird dinosaurs but found in birds.
facts.quote: The deformities of the humerus and the third finger may have been due to osteodysplasia, which had not been reported from non-avian dinosaurs before, but is known in birds.

facts.statement: Because all injuries were healed, the Dilophosaurus survived for months or perhaps years after sustaining these traumas.
facts.quote: Since all the injuries had healed, it is certain that the Dilophosaurus survived for a long time after these events, for months, perhaps years.

facts.statement: The dinosaur's ability to use its forelimbs for catching prey was likely impaired while the injuries healed.
facts.quote: The use of the forelimbs for prey capture must have been compromised during the healing process.

facts.statement: During recovery, the dinosaur likely fasted for a long time or ate only small prey it could kill with its mouth and feet or a single forelimb.
facts.quote: The dinosaur may therefore have endured a long period of fasting or subsisted on prey that was small enough for it to dispatch with the mouth and feet, or with one forelimb.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that enduring pain in multiple body parts for long periods indicates Dilophosaurus was a very hardy animal.
facts.quote: According to Senter and Juengst, the high degree of pain the dinosaur might have experienced in multiple locations for long durations also shows that it was a hardy animal.

facts.statement: It is debated whether paleopathological features are often omitted from descriptions because they focus on normal characteristics or because the features are hard to spot.
facts.quote: They suggested that such features may sometimes be omitted because descriptions of species are concerned with their characteristics rather than abnormalities, or because such features are difficult to recognize.

facts.statement: Dilophosaurus lived during the Early Jurassic, approximately 196 to 186 million years ago.
facts.quote: Dilophosaurus is known from the Kayenta Formation, which dates to the Sinemurian-Toarcian stages of the Early Jurassic, approximately 196–186 million years ago

facts.statement: The species existed for a geological range of 15 million years.
facts.quote: The taxon had a chronostratigraphic range of 15 million years

facts.statement: Fossils of Dilophosaurus have been found in the Kayenta Formation, located in northern Arizona, southeastern Utah, western Colorado, and northwestern New Mexico.
facts.quote: The Kayenta Formation is part of the Glen Canyon Group that includes formations in northern Arizona, parts of southeastern Utah, western Colorado, and northwestern New Mexico

facts.statement: Dilophosaurus lived in a seasonally dry environment featuring migrating sand dunes and river oases lined with conifers.
facts.quote: The environment was seasonally dry, with sand dunes migrating in and out of the wet environments where animals lived, and has been likened to a river oasis

facts.statement: Dilophosaurus was one of the first large predatory dinosaurs, reaching about 7 meters in length and weighing approximately 400 kilograms.
facts.quote: Con aproximadamente 7 m de longitud y con un peso de aproximadamente 400 kilogramos, Dilophosaurus fue uno de los primeros dinosaurios depredadores grandes

facts.statement: The animal had a slender, light build with a proportionally large but delicate skull.
facts.quote: Era delgado y de constitución ligera, y el cráneo era proporcionalmente grande, pero delicado

facts.statement: Dilophosaurus possessed a pair of longitudinal plate-like crests on its skull, similar to those of a cassowary.
facts.quote: Tenía un par de crestas longitudinales en forma de placa en su cráneo, similar a un casuario con dos crestas

facts.statement: Its teeth were long, curved, thin, and laterally compressed.
facts.quote: Los dientes eran largos, curvados, delgados y comprimidos hacia los lados

facts.statement: The hands had four fingers: the first was short but strong with a large claw, the next two were longer and thinner with smaller claws, and the fourth was vestigial.
facts.quote: Las manos tenían cuatro dedos: el primero era corto pero fuerte y tenía una garra grande, los dos dedos siguientes eran más largos y delgados con garras más pequeñas, y el cuarto era vestigial

facts.statement: The arms were powerful, featuring a long and slender humerus bone.
facts.quote: Los brazos eran poderosos, con un hueso del brazo largo y delgado

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Dilophosaurus was active and bipedal, potentially hunting large animals as well as smaller prey and fish.
facts.quote: Dilophosaurus habría sido activo y bípedo, y puede haber cazado animales grandes y también podría haberse alimentado de animales y peces más pequeños

facts.statement: The function of the crests is unknown; they were too weak for combat but may have been used for visual displays, species recognition, or sexual selection.
facts.quote: La función de las crestas es desconocida, eran demasiado débiles para la batalla, pero pueden haber sido utilizados en la visualización, como el reconocimiento de especies y la selección sexual

facts.statement: The species may have grown rapidly, reaching a growth rate of 30 to 35 kilograms per year early in life.
facts.quote: Puede haber crecido rápidamente, alcanzando una tasa de crecimiento de 30 a 35 kilogramos por año al comienzo de su vida

facts.statement: The holotype specimen exhibited multiple paleopathologies, including healed injuries and signs of developmental anomalies.
facts.quote: El espécimen holotipo tenía múltiples paleopatologías, incluyendo lesiones cicatrizadas y signos de una anomalía del desarrollo

facts.statement: The first specimens were described in 1954, but the genus received its current name a decade later.
facts.quote: Los primeros especímenes fueron descritos en 1954, pero no fue hasta una década más tarde que el género recibió su nombre actual

facts.statement: There is a debate among paleontologists regarding whether Dilophosaurus is a basal genus that gave rise to clades like ceratosaurians and tetanurans, or if it is merely a large coelophysid.
facts.quote: Los paleontólogos, consideraron que el Dilophosaurus podría ser un género basal que generó clados como los ceratosaurios y los tetanuros. Otros paleontólogos, piensan al contrario que en realidad este género no es más que un celofísido de gran tamaño

facts.statement: Welles analyzed the taphonomy of the original specimens, detailing changes that occurred during decay and fossilization.
facts.quote: Welles outlined the taphonomy of the original specimens, changes that happened during their decay and fossilization

facts.statement: Welles concluded the specimens were buried near their death sites with little transport, though the holotype shows signs of scavenger disturbance such as rotated vertebrae and a crushed skull.
facts.quote: Welles concluded that the specimens were buried at the place of their deaths, without having been transported much, but that the holotype specimen appears to have been disturbed by scavengers, indicated by the rotated dorsal vertebrae and crushed skull

facts.statement: Dilophosaurus was designated the state dinosaur of Connecticut in 2017.
facts.quote: Fue designado como el dinosaurio estatal de Connecticut en 2017

facts.statement: Dilophosaurus was one of the first large predatory dinosaurs, a medium-sized theropod, though small compared to later theropods.
facts.quote: Dilophosaurus fue uno de los primeros dinosaurios depredadores grandes, un terópodo de tamaño mediano, aunque pequeño en comparación con algunos de los terópodos posteriores.

facts.statement: It had a slender, light build with a size comparable to a brown bear.
facts.quote: Esbelto y de constitución ligera, su tamaño era comparable al de un oso pardo.

facts.statement: The largest known specimen weighed about 400 kg, measured about 7 meters long, and had a skull 590 mm long.
facts.quote: El espécimen más grande conocido pesaba unos 400 kg, medía unos 7 metros de largo, y su cráneo tenía 590 milímetros de largo.

facts.statement: Its most distinctive feature was a pair of rounded crests on its skull, possibly used for display.
facts.quote: La característica más distintiva de Dilophosaurus es el par de crestas redondeadas en su cráneo, usado posiblemente para la exhibición.

facts.statement: In 1997, Dodson noted that cranial crests appeared earlier in Dilophosaurus than in other types of theropods.
facts.quote: En 1997 Dodson notó que las crestas craneales aparecieron antes en el Dilophosaurus que en otros tipos de terópodos.

facts.statement: Its teeth were long but had a fairly small base and flared basally.
facts.quote: Los dientes del Dilophosaurus son largos, pero tienen una base bastante pequeña y se amplían basalmente.

facts.statement: Another skull feature was a notch behind the first row of teeth, giving Dilophosaurus an almost crocodile-like appearance similar to supposedly piscivorous spinosaurids.
facts.quote: Otra característica del cráneo era una muesca detrás de la primera fila de dientes, dando a Dilophosaurus casi un aspecto de cocodrilo, similar a los dinosaurios supuestamente piscívoros espinosáuridos.

facts.statement: This skull structure led to the early hypothesis that Dilophosaurus was a scavenger, with front teeth too weak to kill and hold large prey.
facts.quote: Esta conformación llevó a la hipótesis temprana que Dilophosaurus era un carroñero, con los dientes delanteros siendo demasiado débiles para derribar y sostener una presa grande.

facts.statement: Some researchers interpret a resting trackway of a Dilophosaurus-like theropod as showing feather impressions around the belly and feet, similar to down.
facts.quote: Algunos investigadores han interpretado que una huella de descanso de un terópodo similar a Dilophosaurus y Liliensternus muestra impresiones de plumas alrededor del vientre y los pies, similar al plumón.

facts.statement: Other researchers interpret these impressions as sedimentological artifacts created as the dinosaur moved, though this does not rule out that the trackmaker had feathers.
facts.quote: Otros investigadores interpretan estas impresiones como artefactos sedimentológicos creados a medida que el dinosaurio se movía, aunque esta interpretación no descarta que el creador de huellas haya tenido plumas.

facts.statement: It had 10 cervical vertebrae in the neck, 14 dorsal vertebrae in the back, and 45 caudal vertebrae in the tail.
facts.quote: Dilophosaurus tenía 10 vértebras cervicales en el cuello, 14 dorsales en la espalda y 45 caudales en la cola.

facts.statement: It had a long neck, probably flexed nearly 90° by the skull and shoulder, holding the skull in a horizontal posture.
facts.quote: Tenía un cuello largo, que probablemente estaba flexionado casi 90° por el cráneo y por el hombro, sosteniendo el cráneo en una postura horizontal.

facts.statement: Cervical vertebrae were unusually light; their centers, the "bodies" of the vertebrae, were hollowed by pleurocoels, depressions on the sides, and centrocoels, cavities inside.
facts.quote: Las vértebras cervicales eran inusualmente ligeras; sus centros, los "cuerpos" de las vértebras, estaban ahuecados por pleurocoelos, depresiones en los lados y centroscoelos, cavidades en el interior.

facts.statement: Dorsal neural spines were also low and expanded forward and backward, forming large sites for ligament insertion.
facts.quote: Las espinas neurales de las vértebras dorsal también eran bajas y se expandieron hacia adelante y hacia atrás, lo que formó grandes sitios de inserción para los ligamentos.

facts.statement: The spines had caps that gave the appearance of a Maltese cross, cruciform, when viewed from above, a distinctive feature of this dinosaur.
facts.quote: Las espinas tenían tapas que daban la apariencia de una cruz de Malta, cruciforme, cuando se ve desde arriba, una característica distintiva de este dinosaurio.

facts.statement: The scapulae were wide, particularly the top part, which was rectangular or square, a unique characteristic.
facts.quote: Los omóplatos eran anchos, particularmente la parte superior, que era rectangular o cuadrada, una característica única.

facts.statement: The hands had four fingers; the first was shorter but stronger than the next two, with a large claw, while the next two were longer and thinner with smaller claws.
facts.quote: Las manos tenían cuatro dedos, el primero era más corto pero más fuerte que los dos dedos siguientes, con una garra grande y los dos dedos siguientes eran más largos y delgados, con garras más pequeñas.

facts.statement: The third finger was reduced, and the fourth was vestigial, retained but without function.
facts.quote: El tercer dedo se redujo, y el cuarto fue vestigial, retenido, pero sin función.

facts.statement: The hind legs were large, with a femur, thigh bone, longer than the tibia, shin bone, the opposite of, for example, Coelophysis.
facts.quote: Las patas traseras eran grandes, con un fémur, hueso del muslo, más largo que la tibia, hueso de la parte inferior de la pierna, lo contrario de, por ejemplo, Coelophysis.

facts.statement: The femur was massive, its axis was sigmoid in shape, curved like an S, and its greater trochanter was centered on the axis.
facts.quote: El fémur fue masivo, su eje era de forma sigmoidea, curvado como una S y su trocánter mayor estaba centrado en el eje.

facts.statement: It had long, robust feet with three well-developed toes that had large claws.
facts.quote: Tenía pies largos y robustos con tres dedos bien desarrollados que tenían grandes garras.

facts.statement: The third toe was the strongest, and the first toe of the foot, the hallux, was retained without touching the ground.
facts.quote: El tercer dedo fue el más fuerte, y el primer dedo del pie más pequeño, el hallux, se mantuvo sin tocar el suelo.

facts.statement: The skull of Dilophosaurus was large relative to the general skeleton but delicate.
facts.quote: El cráneo de Dilophosaurus era grande en proporción al esqueleto general, pero delicado.

facts.statement: Dilophosaurus had a pair of high, thin, arched crests or a longitudinal plate on the top of the skull.
facts.quote: Dilophosaurus tenía un par de crestas altas, delgadas y arqueadas o en forma de placa longitudinalmente en el techo del cráneo.

facts.statement: Each crest had a distinctive backward-pointing projection similar to a finger.
facts.quote: Como característica distintiva, cada cresta también tenía una proyección hacia atrás similar a un dedo.

facts.statement: It is unknown if the crest shapes differ between individuals because only one specimen preserves their form.
facts.quote: Como solo un espécimen preserva la forma de las crestas, se desconoce si difieren en otros individuos.

facts.statement: The nasal openings were positioned further back than in most other theropods.
facts.quote: Las fosas nasales se colocaron más atrás que en la mayoría de los otros terópodos.

facts.statement: The subnarial gap resulted in a diastema, a space in the row of teeth, also called a notch.
facts.quote: La brecha subnarial dio como resultado una diastema, un espacio en la fila de dientes, que también se ha denominado "muesca".

facts.statement: The eye socket was oval and narrow towards the bottom.
facts.quote: La órbita era ovalada, y estrecha hacia la parte inferior.

facts.statement: The first specimens of Dilophosaurus wetherilli were described in 1954, but the genus received its current name a decade later.
facts.quote: Los primeros especímenes de Dilophosaurus wetherilli fueron descritos en 1954, pero no fue hasta una década más tarde que el género recibió su nombre actual.

facts.statement: It lived in the Kayenta Formation alongside dinosaurs like Megapnosaurus and Sarahsaurus during the Early Jurassic, approximately 183 million years ago.

facts.quote: Parent group: Neotheropoda

facts.statement: It is classified in the class Reptilia.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia
